name: Dregamine
manufacturer: the Gray Zone opportunists; no consistent manufacturer
description: Not a recipe so much as a category — Dregamine refers to any cocktail of expired, mixed, or degraded legitimate pharmaceuticals cooked down together, typically whatever's been stolen from medical waste, raided from expired stock, or bought from corrupt clinic workers. The name refers to the dregs of the pharmaceutical world. Every batch is different. The base usually contains degraded benzodiazepines, expired stimulants, and whatever pain management compounds happened to be in the haul. Effects and dangers vary wildly by batch.
effects: variable — typically some combination of: sedation, stimulation, mild euphoria, pain relief, anxiety reduction
experienced users learn to identify batch characteristics by taste and color
some batches produce genuinely pleasant mixed effects
cheap and accessible above all else
side_effects: profoundly unpredictable — each batch is a gamble
pharmaceutical interactions between degraded compounds can be toxic
expired benzodiazepines can degrade into toxic metabolites
overdose is common due to inconsistent potency
liver and kidney stress from compound load
cultural_context: Dregamine is what you take when you can't afford anything else — it's the floor of the Gray Zone drug market. Experienced users develop real expertise in reading batches, and 'Dregs tasters' have informal status in some communities — people who can identify what's in a batch before others use it. Deaths from bad batches are regular occurrences. There's dark humor around it: 'What's in the dregs today?' is a morning greeting in some blocks.
story_hooks: Someone has begun deliberately seeding medical waste streams with a specific compound that makes Dregamine batches more addictive — a calculated market-creation scheme targeting the Gray Zone
A Dregs taster has identified a batch containing compounds that shouldn't exist yet — experimental Helix Biosystems formulations that aren't supposed to be in clinical trials for another two years

A Tier 2 clinic worker who's been selling expired stock to Dregamine cooks has a crisis of conscience after a child dies — they have evidence that would expose a network of corrupt medical supply chain workers
